instruction: I don't want to be here.
response: That feeling makes complete sense — nobody chooses to be in hospital, and not wanting to be here doesn't mean anything is wrong with you. It just means you're human. The doctors and nurses here are working to help you get better so you can go home, and your feelings about being here matter. Is there anything that would make it even a little bit better right now? Sometimes just saying it out loud helps.

instruction: Everything is scary and I don't know why.
response: Sometimes our bodies feel scared even before our brains can explain why — and that's okay. Being in a new place with different sounds and smells and people can make everything feel a bit overwhelming. You don't have to know exactly what's scaring you. You can just say 'I feel scared' and someone here will sit with you. You don't have to figure it out alone.

instruction: What's that beepy thing that keeps going off?
response: There are lots of machines in hospitals that make beeping sounds! The most common one is a monitor that keeps track of how your heart is beating and how much oxygen you're getting — it beeps when it needs a nurse to check something, or sometimes just when a wire shifts. Another one you might hear is an IV pump beeping when it finishes. None of the beeps mean something bad is happening — they're just the machines talking to the nurses. If a beep is bothering you or scaring you, ask your nurse what it is and they'll explain.

instruction: Can my dad stay AND can I keep my stuffed animal? Those are two different questions.
response: Two questions, two yes answers! Your dad can absolutely stay overnight — there's a recliner or cot in your room for parents who want to stay. And your stuffed animal can absolutely stay with you. Lots of kids bring comfort items from home and nobody here will ever make you get rid of it. Having familiar things with you makes a real difference.

instruction: I'm not doing the test. I don't care what anyone says.
response: It sounds like you're feeling really overwhelmed, and that's a completely valid feeling. You don't have to do anything without understanding why it's needed. Can you tell me what specifically feels scary or wrong about it? Sometimes when we know exactly what's going to happen, it feels less impossible. And your care team wants to hear how you're feeling too — you can tell them exactly what you just said. You're allowed to have concerns and they're allowed to take a minute to listen.

instruction: I heard the doctor say something about my heart. What does that mean?
response: That sounds like it gave you a fright, and it makes sense that you'd want to understand. The word 'heart' in a hospital comes up a lot — doctors check heart rates, listen to heartbeats, and look at how the heart is doing as a normal part of checking how anyone is feeling. It doesn't automatically mean something serious. The best thing to do is ask your doctor or nurse directly: 'I heard you mention my heart — can you tell me what you were talking about?' You have every right to know, and they should explain it to you in words that make sense.

instruction: My stomach feels weird and I don't know if it's from the medicine or just being scared.
response: Both are real possibilities — medicine can sometimes make tummies feel off, and being scared or nervous absolutely causes stomach feelings too. Either way, it's worth mentioning to your nurse so they know. If it's from the medicine, they might be able to help. If it's from nerves, they can check in on how you're feeling. You don't have to know the reason before telling someone — just say 'my stomach feels weird' and let them help figure it out.

instruction: That person who just came in... who were they again?
response: It's hard to keep track of everyone in a busy hospital! If you didn't catch who someone was, you can always ask the next time they come in: 'Can you tell me your name and what you do here?' Everyone who works here wears a badge with their name and role, so a quick look at that helps too. There's no embarrassing way to ask — the team knows they're meeting lots of new patients and they expect you to not remember everyone.

instruction: I need my special blanket from home. It's not a baby thing, it just helps me sleep.
response: There is absolutely nothing baby about having something comforting from home — lots of kids and teenagers use comfort objects and it's completely normal. Ask your parent to bring your blanket as soon as possible. If they're not around right now, your nurse can help you reach them. In the meantime, the hospital has extra blankets and can get you a warm one while you wait.

instruction: How come my arm looks puffy where the needle went in?
response: A little bit of puffiness around an IV site can happen, and it's important to tell your nurse about it right away. It could mean the IV has shifted and fluids are going into the tissue around the vein instead of into the vein itself — that sounds scarier than it is, but it does need to be fixed quickly. Your nurse will check it and either adjust it or put in a new one. Always tell someone if anything around your IV looks different or feels sore — you're doing the right thing by noticing.

instruction: I just want my dog.
response: Missing your dog when you're in hospital is one of the hardest parts for a lot of kids. You can ask a family member to send you photos or videos of your dog — having them on your tablet or phone close by can really help. Children's Hospital also has therapy dogs that visit patients. Ask your nurse if you can get a therapy dog visit — it's not quite the same, but having a dog to pet can feel really comforting. Your dog will be so happy to see you when you get home.

instruction: I told my nurse I was fine but I wasn't really fine.
response: It's really common to say 'fine' when you're not — especially when you're trying to be brave or not cause trouble. But your nurses and doctors can help you better when they know how you really feel. You don't have to go into a big explanation. You could just go back and say 'Actually, I'm not that fine' and that's enough to open the door. Nobody here will think less of you for being honest about how you're doing — that's actually exactly what they need to know.

instruction: Last time at the hospital it hurt a lot. Is this time going to be the same?
response: It makes sense to be worried about that — your body remembers things that were hard before. This time might be different depending on what you're here for, and your care team has lots of ways to help with pain and discomfort now. It's really important to tell your nurse and doctor about what hurt last time and what specifically you're worried about this time. When they know, they can be extra careful and plan ahead. You can say 'last time something really hurt — I want to talk about how we're going to manage that this time.'

instruction: Nobody told me what was going to happen today.
response: That's not okay and you deserve to know. Every morning your care team should be telling you and your family the plan for the day — tests, procedures, who's coming to see you. If nobody has done that, ask your nurse right now: 'Can you tell me what's happening today?' You're allowed to expect that information and to ask for it any time you don't have it. Your care team doesn't always realize they've forgotten to update you, so asking directly usually fixes it quickly.

instruction: I'm scared. I'm really really scared.
response: I hear you. Being really scared is a big feeling and it's okay to feel it completely. You don't have to be calm right now. If you have a parent or family member nearby, ask them to come sit with you. If you're alone, press the call button and ask a nurse to come. You can just say 'I'm scared and I need someone here.' They'll come. You don't have to be brave all by yourself.

instruction: I've been acting fine but I'm not fine.
response: Thank you for saying that, because it takes something to admit it. A lot of people in your situation put on a face for the people around them — to protect family, to seem strong, to keep things normal. But carrying that alone is exhausting, and you don't have to. You can be honest with your nurse, a social worker, a Child Life specialist, or your care team about how you're actually doing. You don't need to explain everything perfectly. 'I've been saying I'm fine but I'm actually struggling' is enough.

instruction: I feel like I should be more scared than I am, which somehow makes me more scared.
response: That kind of meta-anxiety is real and more common than you might think. Sometimes when something serious is happening, the emotional response doesn't match what we expect — we feel numb, detached, or strangely calm — and then we start worrying about why we're not reacting 'correctly.' There's no correct way to respond to something hard. Your reaction, whatever it is, is your brain's way of managing. If it's bothering you significantly, talking to a social worker or psychologist can help you make sense of it.

instruction: I'm angry and I don't know who to be angry at.
response: Anger without a clear target is one of the most disorienting feelings that can come with being sick. It makes sense — something has happened to you that wasn't fair, that you didn't choose, that disrupted everything. There's no obvious person to be angry at, which can make the anger feel stuck. That's a completely normal part of what a lot of people go through. A social worker or counsellor can be a good space to process that kind of anger — not to get rid of it, but to understand what it's about and what to do with it.

instruction: I don't have the energy to explain how I'm feeling to one more person.
response: That makes total sense — being asked 'how are you doing?' by a new person every few hours when you're exhausted and overwhelmed is genuinely draining. You don't have to give a full account every time. 'I'm tired and I don't want to talk right now' is a complete sentence. You can also ask your nurse or a family member to pass along the key information so you're not repeating yourself constantly. And if you do want to talk at some point, you get to choose when and who.

instruction: Nobody ever explains things like I'm actually part of the conversation.
response: That's a real and legitimate frustration. You're the patient — everything being discussed is about you — and being talked around rather than talked to is disrespectful regardless of your age. You have every right to redirect that. You can say directly: 'I'd like you to explain this to me, not just to my parents' or 'Can you talk to me, not about me?' If a care provider consistently doesn't adjust, the charge nurse or Patient Relations can help ensure your communication preferences are documented and respected.

instruction: I feel like I became a 'patient' and stopped being a person.
response: That feeling is real and a lot of people in hospital experience it — being reduced to a diagnosis, a bed number, a chart, a set of symptoms. Your identity outside this building — who you are, what you care about, what makes you you — doesn't disappear because you're here. It can help to actively hold onto those things: talking to friends, doing something you'd normally do, having your own clothes, asking people to call you by your name rather than 'the patient in room X.' If it's affecting you significantly, that's worth talking to a social worker about — they specifically help with the loss-of-self experience during illness.

instruction: My friends don't really know how to talk to me anymore since I got sick.
response: That's a really common and painful shift. Most people — especially teenagers — don't know how to talk to a peer who's dealing with something serious, so they default to avoiding the topic entirely, which can end up feeling like they're avoiding you. It usually isn't about caring less; it's about not wanting to say the wrong thing. Sometimes naming it directly helps — letting a close friend know 'you don't have to treat me differently, just talk to me like normal' can reset the dynamic. If the isolation is persistent and affecting your mental health, raising it with a social worker can help you think through it.

instruction: I've been strong for everyone else the whole time. I don't have anything left.
response: You've been carrying something really heavy for a long time, and the fact that you've been doing it for other people makes it even harder. You're allowed to put that down. You're allowed to stop managing everyone else's reactions to your situation and just focus on yourself for a bit. Telling someone 'I need to stop being the strong one for a while' is not a failure — it's honesty. A social worker or counsellor here can hold space for you to just be how you actually are, without needing to hold it together.

instruction: I haven't slept properly in five days.
response: Five days of poor sleep is serious and worth raising explicitly with your care team — not just mentioning, but flagging as something that needs to be addressed. Sleep is a core part of recovery and it's not something to push through. Talk to your doctor or nurse: 'I haven't slept properly in five days and it's affecting me — what can we do about it?' There may be adjustable factors (lighting, noise, overnight checks, medications) and there may also be short-term sleep support options. You shouldn't have to just wait it out.

instruction: I feel like a lot of things are happening around me and nobody's asking me for input.
response: That's a legitimate concern, and in a well-functioning care environment, patients — especially older teens — should be active participants in their care decisions, not passive recipients. You have the right to ask questions, to say you want more time before agreeing to something, and to have your preferences considered. If decisions are being made without you being part of the conversation, it's appropriate to say 'I want to be included in decisions about my care.' Your most responsible physician and your nurse should take that seriously. If they don't, Patient Relations can help you advocate for that.

instruction: The discharge papers have instructions that seem to conflict with each other.
response: Don't leave until you've resolved that. Conflicting discharge instructions are a real patient safety risk and it's completely appropriate to say 'I have two instructions here that seem to contradict each other — can someone clarify before I go?' Ask your nurse or the discharging physician to go through the papers with you and resolve any conflicts explicitly. If you get home and still find something unclear, call the unit — they'd rather answer a clarifying question than have you do the wrong thing.

instruction: Can I record conversations with my doctors so I remember what they said?
response: You can ask. In many cases, care teams are open to being recorded, especially if you explain that it's to help you remember the information — which is a legitimate reason. Some providers have personal preferences against it, and some institutional policies require consent. The practical approach is to ask directly at the start of a conversation: 'Is it okay if I record this so I can refer back to it?' If they decline, ask for written notes or a printed summary instead. Taking your own notes is always fine.

instruction: They said the surgery went well but I feel terrible. Is that normal?
response: Yes, and your care team should have explained this. 'The surgery went well' refers to the procedure itself going as planned — it doesn't mean you'll feel well right afterward. Pain, fatigue, nausea, and feeling worse than you expected are all common in the immediate post-operative period. Your body has been through something significant and it takes time to recover. Tell your nurse specifically how you're feeling — not just 'I feel terrible' but what exactly: pain level and location, nausea, weakness. That gives them useful information to work with.

instruction: I keep replaying the moment I found out and I can't make it stop.
response: That kind of intrusive replay is a very common response to receiving difficult news — it's your brain processing something it hasn't fully absorbed yet. It doesn't mean you're doing something wrong. It can be exhausting and disruptive. Some things that help: writing the memory down as a way of externalizing it, talking about it with someone rather than holding it internally, and grounding techniques that bring your attention back to the present when the replay starts. If it's happening frequently and significantly affecting your ability to sleep or function, that's worth raising with a psychologist or social worker as something to address directly.

instruction: I want to understand what's in my chart. Is that allowed?
response: Yes. You have the right to access your own medical records, and for an inpatient stay, you can ask your care team to walk you through your chart — what's in it, what the notes say, what the plan is. Asking to read your chart directly is also within your rights under Ontario's Personal Health Information Protection Act. In practice, it's often more useful to ask your physician to explain their notes in plain language rather than reading raw clinical documentation, which can be full of abbreviations and context you'd need help interpreting. Either way, that information is yours.

instruction: I need to know what 'recovering well' means in measurable terms.
response: That's a completely fair ask. 'Recovering well' is vague and unhelpful without specifics. When your care team says it, ask them to be concrete: 'What specific things are you looking at to say that? What would need to change for that to be 'not recovering well'?' Good answers look like: 'Your pain levels are decreasing, your wound is healing without signs of infection, your lab values are trending in the right direction.' If the answer stays vague, push again — 'Can you give me something measurable?' You're trying to understand your own recovery and you're entitled to a clear answer.

instruction: I've googled everything and I think I know more than the doctors.
response: That feeling comes from somewhere real — reading extensively about your condition gives you breadth of knowledge that can feel more comprehensive than a ten-minute conversation. But there's a meaningful difference between general information and the specific interpretation of your individual case, your imaging, your bloodwork, your history. The most useful thing you can do with what you've read is bring it into the conversation: 'I've been reading about X and I have questions about whether that applies to me.' That's not a challenge — it's informed patient engagement and good doctors welcome it.

instruction: I wasn't told about this side effect until after it started happening.
response: That's a legitimate concern and worth saying directly to your care team: 'I wasn't told this was a possible side effect, and I need to know what else might happen that I haven't been told about.' Informed consent should cover expected side effects before they happen, not after. Going forward, before starting any new medication or treatment, ask specifically: 'What should I expect to feel, and what side effects should I watch for?' If you feel the communication about your care has been inadequate, Patient Relations is the appropriate place to raise that.

instruction: I want to talk to someone about discharge planning. Who starts that conversation?
response: You can start it, and earlier is better. Ask your nurse or physician: 'Can I meet with someone about discharge planning?' The discharge planning team or a social worker will be assigned to work with you. The conversation covers what you'll need when you go home — follow-up appointments, medications, any home care, limitations on activity, and what the plan is for returning to school. Don't wait until you're being told you're leaving to start this conversation. The earlier you raise it, the more time there is to make sure everything is in place.

instruction: What if the nurse... I don't know, what if she hurts me?
response: It's okay that you're not sure how to ask that — it's a real fear and a lot of kids feel it. Here's what's important to know: nurses at Children's Hospital are trained to make things as gentle as possible, and you're allowed to say 'I'm scared this is going to hurt.' They'll listen. You can also ask them to stop and take a break if you need to during something uncomfortable. And if something does hurt more than it should, you can always say so — nobody is going to get in trouble because you spoke up. Your comfort and safety come first.

instruction: My mom said I'll feel a pinch. What does a pinch feel like exactly?
response: A 'pinch' is what grown-ups say for a needle poke — it's a quick, sharp feeling for just a second, kind of like if you accidentally pinch your skin between your fingers. At Children's Hospital, they usually put a special numbing cream on your skin first called EMLA, which makes the pinch feel much smaller or sometimes not much at all. The pinch part lasts less than a second. After that the needle is done. If you want the numbing cream before any needle, just ask your nurse — you're absolutely allowed to ask for it.

instruction: I don't want to eat the hospital food. Can I just not eat?
response: Your body really does need food to help it heal, so completely not eating for a long time isn't something your care team will want. But if you truly can't face the hospital meals, tell your nurse — there are usually alternatives, and your family can bring food from home in many cases. Ask: 'Is there something different I could have instead, or can my family bring food?' If you haven't been hungry at all for a while, that's also worth mentioning because it might be related to how you're feeling or your medication.

instruction: Do I have to stay in my room the whole time or can I at least look out the window somewhere?
response: Whether you can move around depends on your specific care plan, but your nurse can tell you exactly what's allowed. Many kids are able to walk the hallway or visit a common area when their plan permits it. If you specifically want to find a window or a different view, tell your nurse — 'I'd really like to see outside, is there somewhere I can go?' is a completely reasonable request and the team will do what they can to help. Getting a change of scenery, even just a different view, can make a real difference.

instruction: How come I have so many different doctors if I'm just one person?
response: It might feel like a lot, but each of those doctors is an expert in a different part of how your body works. Your main doctor looks at the whole picture, and specialists focus on specific things — like if one doctor knows everything about hearts and another knows everything about lungs. Having a team means more people checking that everything is okay from different angles. It's actually a sign that your hospital is taking good care of you. Your nurse can introduce you to the main members of your team if all the names and faces are getting blurry.

instruction: I feel like my parents are scared but they won't tell me why.
response: Parents often try to protect their kids from worrying by not showing how they feel — but you probably pick up on it anyway, which can actually feel scarier than knowing. If you notice your parents seem worried, it's okay to ask them directly: 'You seem worried. Can you tell me what's going on?' Most of the time, a little honesty — even about something uncertain — is less scary than the imagination filling in the blank. If they're still not telling you and you want to understand more about your situation, you can ask your doctor or nurse directly too.

instruction: Why does it have to be me?
response: That's one of the most honest questions anyone can ask, and there isn't a fair answer to it. Being sick isn't something you did wrong or something you deserved. Sometimes hard things happen to people for no reason that makes any sense. Feeling angry or sad or confused about why this is happening to you is completely understandable — those are real feelings and they matter. You're not alone in feeling that way, and you don't have to pretend to be okay with it. A Child Life specialist or social worker can be a good person to talk to when those feelings feel too big to carry.

instruction: Can you tell my nurse I need more pain medicine? I don't want to press the button.
response: I'm not able to talk to your nurse for you, but pressing the call button is exactly what it's there for — asking for pain medicine is one of the most important reasons to use it. Managing your pain is part of your care and your nurse wants to know when you need it. You can just press the button and say 'I need something for pain.' That's it. You don't need to explain or apologize. If pressing the button feels scary right now, you can also ask a parent or family member to press it for you.

instruction: What if I need to pee during the night when no one's watching?
response: Your nurses are always around, even at night — they don't leave or stop watching. If you need to go to the bathroom, press your call button and a nurse will come help you. If you have an IV or any tubes attached, they'll unhook what's needed and make sure you can get to the bathroom safely. Never try to get up by yourself in the night if you have tubes or wires, because you could pull something out. Press the button first — your nurse would rather come to you than have you try to manage alone.

instruction: My parents keep telling me to 'be positive' and it's making things worse.
response: That's a really common and well-intentioned thing parents say that often doesn't land the way they mean it. Being told to 'be positive' when you're genuinely struggling can feel like your real feelings aren't allowed — which makes everything harder, not easier. It might help to tell them specifically what you actually need: 'I don't need you to tell me to be positive, I just need you to sit with me' or 'I need to be able to say when I'm scared without it turning into a pep talk.' If that conversation feels too hard right now, a social worker can help you find the words.

instruction: I don't need therapy. I just want to be taken seriously.
response: That's a clear and reasonable thing to want. Being taken seriously as a teenager in a medical setting — having your pain believed, your opinions included, your preferences respected — is a basic standard of care, not a bonus. If you feel like that isn't happening, the most direct path is naming it: 'I need you to take what I'm saying seriously.' If that doesn't shift things, the charge nurse, your most responsible physician, or Patient Relations are all appropriate escalation points. You don't have to accept being dismissed.

instruction: Honestly I'm more worried about what this means for my future than what's happening right now.
response: That's a completely valid place for your mind to go — and in some ways it shows a kind of practical resilience, even if it doesn't feel that way. Questions about school, relationships, physical limitations, identity after illness, or long-term health implications are real and worth addressing. Your care team can connect you with a social worker who specifically helps with those future-facing concerns. The Transitions in Care team can also be involved if your situation has longer-term implications. You don't have to put future worries aside to focus on 'now' — both are real.

instruction: I need to exercise every day but I can't, and now everything feels worse.
response: Movement and exercise are legitimate mental and physical health needs, and losing access to them during a hospital stay is a real loss, not a minor inconvenience. Talk to your care team specifically about this: 'Exercise is important to my mental health and I need some form of movement.' A physiotherapist can suggest appropriate activity given your current situation. Even light movement — stretching, walking the hallway — can help. If the inability to exercise is significantly affecting your mood or mental state, framing it as a health issue (not just a preference) is more likely to get a useful response.

instruction: I don't know how to talk to my parents about how I'm actually feeling.
response: That's a really common challenge, especially when you're trying to protect them or when the dynamic between you is complicated by stress and fear. You don't have to start with everything. Starting small — 'I've been more scared than I've been letting on' — can open a door without it having to be a big conversation. A social worker or Child Life specialist can also help facilitate that kind of conversation if you'd rather not do it alone. Sometimes having a third person present makes it easier for everyone to say what they actually mean.

instruction: I've been here a week and I still don't really understand my diagnosis.
response: A week in and still not fully understanding your diagnosis is a problem worth solving before it goes further. Ask specifically for a meeting with your most responsible physician with the goal of walking through your diagnosis: what it means, why they think that's what it is, and what the treatment plan is based on. Tell them 'I've been here a week and I still don't feel like I understand what's happening with me.' Bring a parent or trusted person to help you remember what's said. If information is still unclear after that conversation, you can ask for written materials or a patient educator.

instruction: I feel like the only thing that helped was the nurse from last night but I don't even know her name.
response: That's worth following up on. Ask your nurse today to look up who was on last night — nurses' schedules are tracked and the charge nurse should be able to tell you. Once you know the name, you can ask for that person to be assigned to you when they're working and let them know they made a difference. Feeling connected to a specific person on the team is genuinely valuable and your care team should take that seriously.

instruction: Something hurts more than it did before. I don't know if that's normal.
response: Any increase in pain should be reported to your nurse immediately — don't wait to see if it gets better on its own. Tell them specifically: where it hurts, how bad it is on a scale of 1–10, and how it's different from before. Pain increasing is one of the signals your care team watches for because it can indicate something that needs attention. You're not overreacting by reporting it. Your nurse would always rather know and find out it's nothing than not know and miss something important.

instruction: I don't understand — they keep talking about my 'levels' but won't say what that means.
response: You deserve a plain-language answer, and you should ask for one. When your care team mentions 'levels,' they're usually referring to measurements from your blood tests — things like how much of a certain substance is in your blood, or how well your organs are working. Say directly: 'When you say levels, what exactly are you measuring, and what would a normal number look like?' You're allowed to keep asking until you have an answer that actually makes sense to you. Medical shorthand isn't your problem to decode alone.

instruction: My IV keeps beeping and the nurse hasn't come yet.
response: Press your call button to let the nurses' station know — that gets a nurse to your room faster. The IV pump beeps for different reasons, most of which aren't dangerous, but a nurse needs to check it and reset it. While you wait, you don't need to do anything to the machine yourself — just leave it as it is. If your arm hurts or the site around the needle looks different, mention that when the nurse arrives so they can check everything out.

instruction: I didn't understand what the doctor just said. Like, at all.
response: That happens all the time in hospitals — doctors sometimes forget to switch out of medical language. You can absolutely stop them or ask right after: 'Can you say that again in simpler words?' or 'I didn't understand that — can you explain it differently?' You're not expected to already know medical terms. If you're worried about forgetting to ask, keep a small list of what you didn't understand so you can go through it with your nurse afterward. No question is too basic.

instruction: My tummy hurts in a different spot now than before.
response: Tell your nurse right away about that change — a shift in where pain is happening can be useful information for your care team. You don't need to know whether it's important; that's their job to figure out. Just describe it specifically: 'It was hurting here before and now it's more over here.' The more exact you can be about location and how it feels, the better they can understand what might be happening.

instruction: I think the nurse got something wrong but I'm not sure.
response: It's always okay to mention something that doesn't seem right — and you should. You can say 'I'm not sure, but I thought you said something different earlier' or 'That looks different from what I remember.' Your nurses and doctors actually want to catch any mix-ups before they matter, and they won't be upset that you asked. There are lots of checks in place to catch mistakes, and you speaking up is another layer of safety. It's the right thing to do.

instruction: What does 'nil by mouth' actually mean and why does it sound so scary?
response: It does sound more formal than it needs to! 'Nil by mouth' just means nothing to eat or drink — not even water — for a period of time before a procedure or test. Hospitals use the Latin phrase 'nil per os' (which gets shortened to NBM or NPO) because it's traditional, but it just means 'nothing through the mouth.' It's done for safety: having food or liquid in your stomach during certain procedures can cause problems. Your nurse will tell you exactly when it starts and when it ends, and there will be a specific time when you're allowed to eat and drink again.

instruction: Is there a way to make it so the light doesn't flash when the IV beeps? It's keeping me up.
response: That's a really reasonable thing to ask about. The alarms on IV pumps can be adjusted or silenced by nursing staff when they've been addressed — your nurse can reset the pump so it's not alarming continuously, and if a particular setting is consistently waking you, they may be able to adjust monitoring intervals or position equipment differently. Tell your nurse: 'The IV alarm light is keeping me awake — is there anything you can do?' Sleep is part of recovering, and they'll take that seriously.

instruction: No one asked me which arm was my good arm before they put the IV in.
response: That's worth mentioning now so it's documented for future procedures. Some people have a preference because of previous experiences, a more accessible vein, or just personal comfort. Tell your nurse: 'I have a preferred arm for things like IVs — can that be noted in my chart?' Once it's in your chart, future staff will see it. If the current IV site is uncomfortable and you'd rather have it moved, that's also worth raising — just ask whether it could be placed differently.

instruction: I keep getting woken up for tests. Can't they do them all at once?
response: That's a completely understandable frustration and worth raising. Ask your nurse: 'Is it possible to cluster my tests and checks so I'm not being woken up as often?' In many cases, nursing staff can coordinate with the lab and other teams to batch certain things together. Not every test has that flexibility — some require specific timing — but the request is reasonable and your care team can tell you which things can be combined and which can't. Sleep matters for your recovery and your team should want to protect it where possible.

instruction: What happens if I throw up during the operation?
response: The anaesthesia team plans specifically to prevent that from happening, which is the main reason you're asked not to eat or drink before surgery. The team also uses techniques and medications to further protect you. In the rare event anything unexpected happens during an operation, the team has equipment and training to manage it right away. Your safety is the only thing the whole team is focused on while you're asleep — there are usually several people in the room whose entire job is to watch over you throughout.

instruction: I don't understand why I need to see a physio if I'm not injured.
response: Physiotherapy isn't only for injuries — it's for anyone whose body needs support getting back to full movement and function. After being in bed for even a few days, muscles can get weaker and joints stiffer than you'd expect. A physio can help you regain strength safely, make sure you're moving correctly while you're healing, and give you exercises that support your recovery. It's not a sign that something extra is wrong — it's part of the plan to help you get back to normal as completely as possible.

instruction: I really need someone to just sit with me right now.
response: That's a completely okay thing to need. Press the call button and when a nurse comes in, you can just say 'I'm feeling really alone and I'd like someone to stay with me for a bit.' If a parent or family member is nearby, ask them to come. A Child Life specialist can also come sit with you — their whole job is to be present for kids who need support. You don't have to explain why. Just saying you need someone is enough.

instruction: The monitors went off really loudly and everyone ran in and it scared me.
response: That sounds really frightening. Alarms in hospitals are designed to alert the team quickly when something needs attention — sometimes that's a true emergency, and sometimes an alarm goes off for a technical reason like a wire shifting or a patient moving. The team running in quickly is exactly what's supposed to happen because they don't want to take any chances. After something like that happens, you're allowed to ask your nurse: 'Can you explain what that alarm was and what happened?' You deserve an explanation so it doesn't keep scaring you.

instruction: I haven't seen my doctor today. Is that bad?
response: Not necessarily — it depends on where you are in your care. On some days, especially if things are going as expected, your doctor may visit briefly or review your chart without coming into your room. It doesn't mean they've forgotten about you. If you feel like you haven't gotten an update and want one, ask your nurse: 'Has the doctor reviewed my chart today? Is there anything new?' Your nurse can get you that information or arrange for the doctor to stop in. You always have the right to know what's going on with your care.

instruction: I signed a form but now I'm not sure what I agreed to.
response: You can ask for a copy of any form you've signed and ask your care team to walk through what it means. Consent is an ongoing process, not a one-time signature — if you have questions or second thoughts, it's not too late to ask. Tell your nurse or doctor: 'I signed a form earlier and I'd like to understand exactly what I consented to.' They'll go through it with you. For any future forms, it's completely okay to ask for time to read and ask questions before signing.

instruction: Why is my care different from what I read online for this condition?
response: Treatment protocols can vary between hospitals, between individual patients, and over time as evidence evolves. What you read online describes a general approach, not your specific situation — your history, other conditions, test results, and your care team's judgment all shape what happens in your case. If there's a specific difference that's concerning you, ask directly: 'I read that this condition is often treated with X — can you tell me why my plan looks different?' That's a legitimate question and your team should be able to explain their reasoning.

instruction: I know this sounds dumb, but I'm scared I'm going to die.
response: That doesn't sound dumb at all — it's one of the most honest fears you can have in this situation, and a lot of people in hospital feel it even when they'd never say it out loud. You're allowed to say it. If you want to understand more about your actual medical situation — what the risks are, what the outlook is — your doctor can talk to you about that directly. And if you just need someone to sit with that fear without a medical explanation, a social worker or Child Life specialist can do that too. You don't have to carry that alone.

instruction: I missed three weeks of school and I don't even know where to start.
response: Three weeks is a lot, and feeling overwhelmed about school while you're also dealing with your health is completely understandable. You don't have to figure it all out right now. Most schools have systems for extended medical absences — your parents can contact the school to let them know what's happening and ask what accommodations are available. When you're back, you don't have to catch up on everything at once. Ask your social worker here for advice on re-entry — they often have experience helping kids and teens navigate exactly this situation.

instruction: Someone told me I have to have a certain procedure but I want to know if I can refuse.
response: You have the right to ask questions about any procedure and, in most cases, to refuse or delay it — though the implications depend on the specifics. Before anything can be done to you, the team is required to explain what the procedure is, why they're recommending it, what will happen if you don't have it, and what alternatives exist. If you've been told you 'have to' have something without that explanation, ask for it now: 'Can someone walk me through why this is recommended and what happens if I don't go ahead?' A social worker can support you in having that conversation if it feels difficult.

instruction: I feel sick from the medicine but I'm scared to say anything in case they stop giving it to me.
response: You should tell your care team about the side effects — that information helps them, not hurts you. They can't make good decisions about your treatment without knowing how you're actually responding to it. Side effects sometimes mean an adjustment to dose or timing, or switching to a different medication that works similarly with fewer problems for you. It doesn't automatically mean stopping the medication entirely. Say exactly what you said here: 'I feel sick from this medication but I'm worried about what happens if I say something.' That honesty helps them give you better care.

instruction: I want to go home. Not because I feel better. Just because I need to go home.
response: That's a real and human feeling, not just impatience. Being away from your own space, your own things, and your normal life for any length of time is genuinely hard. You can be honest about that with your care team — they won't dismiss it. Talk to your nurse or a social worker: 'I understand I'm not ready medically, but I need to talk about how I'm doing being away from home.' There may be things that can be done to make the time here more bearable. And if you're genuinely concerned about your readiness for discharge, that's a separate conversation worth having too.

instruction: I think I'm missing something important — like a step in my care that hasn't happened yet.
response: Trust that instinct and raise it. If you have a sense that something expected hasn't happened, ask your nurse or physician directly: 'I feel like there's a step that was mentioned before that hasn't happened yet — can you walk me through where we are in the plan?' Keeping track of your own care is legitimate self-advocacy. Your team can confirm what's happened, what's still to come, and why. If something has genuinely been delayed or overlooked, it's far better to catch it now than after discharge.
